questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis vs Euthyroid Hyperthyroxinemia & Iodine Effects
questions.q: How does page 910 distinguish thyrotoxicosis from euthyroid hyperthyroxinemia in patients with elevated T3 and T4 levels?

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis vs Euthyroid Hyperthyroxinemia & Iodine Effects

questions.sec: Thyrotoxicosis vs Euthyroid Hyperthyroxinemia & Iodine Effects

questions.sec: Antibodies, Triad of Manifestations & Clinical Presentation

questions.exp: TRAb is positive in 80-95% (most important in Graves); Thyroglobulin Ab in 50-70% (most important in Hashimoto); TPO Ab in 50-80%. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Antibodies, Triad of Manifestations & Clinical Presentation
questions.q: TSH-Receptor antibodies stimulate T-cells, fibroblasts, and GAG synthesis to produce which triad of unique clinical findings in Graves' disease?

Thyroid ophthalmopathy, Thyroid dermopathy (pretibial myxedema), and Thyroid acropachy
Periorbital edema, macroglossia, and hoarse voice
Carpal tunnel syndrome, delayed reflexes, and bradycardia
questions.exp: TRAb stimulates T-cells, fibroblasts, and GAGs, leading to the unique triad of Graves: Thyroid ophthalmopathy, Thyroid Dermopathy (Pretibial myxedema), and Thyroid Acropachy. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Antibodies, Triad of Manifestations & Clinical Presentation
questions.q: Match the unique physical findings of Graves' disease shown in the photographs — 1) Eye pathology 2) Lower extremity dermopathy 3) Digits … A) Severe proptosis, eyelid retraction, and exophthalmos B) Pretibial myxedema (thick nodular infiltrative dermopathy) C) Acropachy
questions.exp: The photographs illustrate proptosis/eyelid retraction/exophthalmos, acropachy, and thick nodular infiltrative dermopathy (pretibial myxedema). (Book p911)

questions.sec: Antibodies, Triad of Manifestations & Clinical Presentation

questions.sec: Antibodies, Triad of Manifestations & Clinical Presentation

questions.exp: Page 911 notes: 'Wt loss + good appetite -> Graves disease' and 'Wt gain + loss of appetite -> Hypothyroid'. (Book p911)

questions.sec: Scintigraphy Grid, Ophthalmopathy Progression & Eponymous Signs

questions.q: Which of the following conditions is NOT associated with an elevated TSH level in the summary note on page 915?
opts: TSH Adenoma and recovery phase of thyroiditis
questions.exp: Central hypothyroidism has a 'Normal TSH level' (with low peripheral hormones); elevated TSH is seen in 1° hypothyroid, RTH, TSH adenoma, and recovery phase of thyroiditis. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute Thyroiditis Triphasic Curve & Postpartum Comparison
questions.q: Per the summary note on page 915, what does a normal TSH level signify in a patient with low circulating thyroid hormones?
opts: Early toxic phase of subacute thyroiditis
questions.exp: Page 915 explicitly states: 'Normal TSH level : Central hypothyroidism'. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute Thyroiditis Triphasic Curve & Postpartum Comparison
questions.q: Postpartum thyroiditis is also known as ___ or ___ thyroiditis.
questions.exp: Under Postpartum thyroiditis: 'AKA Painless / silent thyroiditis'. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute Thyroiditis Triphasic Curve & Postpartum Comparison
questions.q: Match the autoimmune diseases associated with postpartum thyroiditis — 1) Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) 2) Sjogren's syndrome 3) Endocrine / skin autoimmune … A) Connective tissue disease B) Exocrine gland sicca syndrome C) Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) / Vitiligo
questions.exp: Postpartum thyroiditis is seen in association with autoimmune diseases: SLE, Sjogren's syndrome, T1DM, and Vitiligo. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute Thyroiditis Triphasic Curve & Postpartum Comparison
questions.q: Compare pain and pregnancy timing in Subacute vs Postpartum thyroiditis: I Neck pain is present in subacute thyroiditis, but absent/silent in postpartum thyroiditis. II Subacute thyroiditis has no association with pregnancy, whereas postpartum thyroiditis occurs post partum.
opts: I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
questions.exp: Table comparisons: Pain is Present in subacute, Absent/silent in postpartum; Association with pregnancy is No in subacute, Post Partum in postpartum. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute Thyroiditis Triphasic Curve & Postpartum Comparison
questions.q: From the subacute vs postpartum thyroiditis comparison table, match the lab/treatment characteristics — 1) ESR 2) Anti-TPO antibody 3) Role of steroids … A) Subacute: ↑↑ ESR; -ve TPO Ab; Steroids: Yes B) Postpartum: Normal ESR; +ve TPO Ab; Steroids: No (β-blocker can be used)
questions.exp: Subacute has ↑↑ ESR, -ve TPO Ab, and steroids are useful (Yes); Postpartum has normal ESR, +ve TPO Ab, and no steroids (β-blockers used). (Book p915)

questions.sec: Subacute Thyroiditis Triphasic Curve & Postpartum Comparison
questions.q: Assess autoimmunity in these thyroiditides: I Subacute thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease. II Postpartum thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease with positive anti-TPO antibodies.
opts: Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
Both I and II are false
I is false; II is true
questions.exp: Table shows: Autoimmune is 'No' for Subacute thyroiditis, and 'Yes' for Postpartum thyroiditis. (Book p915)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: Amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism is typically a transient phenomenon mediated by which physiological mechanism?
opts: Wolff-Chaikoff phenomenon due to massive iodine load
questions.exp: Under Amiodarone induces: Hypothyroidism is a 'Transient phenomenon' 'D/t Wolff chaikoff phenomenon'. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: Match the type of amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis to its underlying pathophysiology — 1) Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis Type-I 2) Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis Type-II … A) Patient with underlying thyroid disease (Graves or MNG); Jod-Basedow phenomenon; ↑↑ vascularity B) No underlying disease; lysosomal-mediated destruction; no antibodies; ↓↓ vascularity
questions.exp: Type I occurs in underlying disease via Jod-Basedow with ↑↑ vascularity; Type II occurs without underlying disease via lysosomal destruction with ↓↓ vascularity. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: What is the medical drug of choice (DOC) for Amiodarone-Induced Thyrotoxicosis Type I versus Type II?
opts: Type I: Radioactive iodine; Type II: High-dose aspirin
Type I: Lithium carbonate; Type II: Potassium iodide
Type I: Thionamides (DOC); Type II: Corticosteroids (Steroids)
Type I: Corticosteroids; Type II: Thionamides
questions.exp: Management: Type-I -> Stop treatment, Start Thionamide (DOC); Type-II -> Drug should be stopped, Rx -> Steroid. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: A 62-year-old man on chronic amiodarone therapy develops thyrotoxicosis. Color Doppler ultrasound demonstrates absent/markedly decreased thyroid vascularity (↓↓ vascularity), and autoantibodies are negative. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
opts: Subacute de Quervain thyroiditis; treat with aspirin
Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis Type II; stop drug and treat with steroids
Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis Type I; treat with thionamides
Graves disease; treat with radioactive iodine ablation
questions.exp: Type II has no underlying disease, no antibodies, markedly decreased vascularity, and is treated by stopping amiodarone and starting steroids. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: In the comparison table on page 916, match the condition to its typical symptom duration — 1) Subacute Thyroiditis 2) Graves' Disease 3) Toxic MNG … A) Days to weeks B) 2 - 3 months C) Months to years
questions.exp: Duration: Subacute Thyroiditis lasts days to weeks; Graves' Disease lasts 2-3 months; Toxic MNG lasts months to years. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: In which entity alone is local neck pain characteristically present in the page 916 comparison grid?
questions.exp: Under Neck pain: Present in Subacute Thyroiditis; Absent in Graves' Disease; Absent in Toxic MNG. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: Match the goiter physical characteristics on page 916 — 1) Subacute Thyroiditis 2) Graves' Disease 3) Toxic MNG … A) Small goiter B) Diffuse goiter C) Nodular goiter
questions.exp: Goiter type: Subacute Thyroiditis = Small; Graves' Disease = Diffuse; Toxic MNG = Nodular. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: Regarding extrathyroidal manifestations (ophthalmopathy and dermopathy): I Present in Graves' disease. II Absent in both Subacute thyroiditis and Toxic multinodular goiter.
opts: Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
questions.exp: Ophthalmopathy / Dermopathy is Absent in Subacute Thyroiditis, Present in Graves' Disease, and Absent in Toxic MNG. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: In differentiating hyperthyroid conditions on page 916, the serum T3/T4 ratio is ___ in subacute thyroiditis, but ___ in both Graves' disease and toxic MNG.
questions.exp: T3/T4 ratio is < 15 in Subacute Thyroiditis, and > 20 in both Graves' Disease and Toxic MNG. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies are characteristically present in which of the three conditions?
opts: Both subacute thyroiditis and toxic MNG
questions.exp: TSH-R stimulating Ab is Absent in Subacute Thyroiditis, Present in Graves' Disease, and Absent in Toxic MNG. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: On ultrasound and color Doppler, what is described as the best test to diagnose Graves' disease on page 916?
opts: Diffusely enlarged gland with markedly increased vascularity (↑↑ vascularity)
Small shrunken gland with absent vascularity
Multiple hypoechoic nodules with peripheral flow
Thick calcified thyroid capsule with acoustic shadowing
questions.exp: Ultrasound for Graves' Disease: 'Diffusely enlarged gland, ↑↑ vascularity (Best test to diagnose)'. (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: Match the radioiodine (RAI) uptake finding to the condition on page 916 — 1) Subacute Thyroiditis 2) Graves' Disease 3) Toxic MNG … A) Low uptake B) Markedly increased (↑↑) uptake C) Depends on functional status of nodules (cold or hot nodules)
questions.exp: Radioiodine uptake: Subacute Thyroiditis = Low uptake; Graves' Disease = ↑↑ uptake; Toxic MNG = Depends on functional status of nodules (cold or hot nodules). (Book p916)

questions.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid
questions.q: Which of the following features is NOT characteristic of Toxic Multinodular Goiter (MNG) in the page 916 table?
opts: Prominent infiltrative ophthalmopathy and pretibial dermopathy
Duration of symptoms spanning months to years
Commonly occurs in the elderly population (Females > Males)
Nodular goiter with enlarged nodules on ultrasound
questions.exp: Ophthalmopathy and dermopathy are absent in toxic MNG; they are present only in Graves' disease. (Book p916)

units.title: Causes of Thyrotoxicosis, Graves Disease & Iodine Effects
units.sec: Thyrotoxicosis vs Euthyroid Hyperthyroxinemia & Iodine Effects · p910
units.guide: Distinguish overworking vs normal gland thyrotoxicosis, demographics and associations of Graves (smoking, postpartum, HAART, HLA-DR2), Wolff-Chaikoff effect (transient 5-7 day inhibition by excess iodide), and Jod-Basedow phenomenon.

units.title: Graves Antibodies, Manifestations & Systemic Features
units.sec: Antibodies, Triad of Manifestations & Clinical Presentation · p911
units.guide: Cover TRAb (80-95%) driving ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxedema, and acropachy; common hyperadrenergic symptoms; elderly apathetic thyrotoxicosis; protein catabolism (proximal myopathy without fasciculations, osteopenia, stones); and hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

units.title: Scintigraphy Patterns, Ophthalmopathy Mnemonic & Eye Signs
units.sec: Scintigraphy Grid, Ophthalmopathy Progression & Eponymous Signs · p912
units.guide: Anchor the scintigraphy table, microscopic scalloped appearance, the 40/40/20 rule, the IM SLOW extraocular muscle mnemonic, eponymous eye signs (Von Graefe, Joffroy, Stellwag, Dalrymple, Möbius), and non-palpable gland causes.

units.title: Laboratory Findings, Anti-Thyroid Drugs, Relapse, RAI & Surgery
units.sec: Ancillary Labs, Thionamides, RAI & Surgical Indications · p913
units.guide: Master thionamide equivalency (methimazole 6 mg = carbimazole 10 mg = PTU 100 mg), PTU in pregnancy, carbimazole 5 mg TDS, methimazole teratogenicity, side effects (rash m/c, agranulocytosis most dangerous), RAI precautions, and surgical indications.

units.title: Thyrotoxic Crisis & Classification of Thyroiditis
units.sec: Thyroid Storm Protocol & Acute, Subacute, Chronic Thyroiditis · p914
units.guide: Review thyroid storm presentation and 4-drug emergency regimen (PTU 1000 mg stat -> 250 mg Q4H, steroid, propranolol 60 mg Q4H, iopanoic acid 500 mg BD), acute suppurative thyroiditis (piriform sinus fistula), de Quervain HLA-B35, and Riedel IgG4 fibrous disease.

units.title: Subacute Thyroiditis Mechanism, Timeline & Postpartum Thyroiditis
units.sec: Subacute Thyroiditis Triphasic Curve & Postpartum Comparison · p915
units.guide: Follow the stored hormone release mechanism (T3/T4 < 15, neck/ear pain, high ESR), aspirin 600 mg Q6H DOC, the 18-week three-phase curve, and the comparison grid with postpartum silent thyroiditis.

units.title: Effects of Amiodarone on Thyroid & Thyroiditis Comparison Grid
units.sec: Amiodarone Type I vs Type II & Differential Diagnosis Grid · p916
units.guide: Contrast Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis Type I (underlying disease, Jod-Basedow, high vascularity, thionamides) vs Type II (destructive, no antibodies, low vascularity, steroids), and master the summary comparison table (subacute vs Graves vs toxic MNG).
